I spent most of the week before the September meeting staring at the same question every rates strategist was asking: how much of this was already in the curve? My honest answer, as of the close on 17 September 2026, was most of it. The hike was roughly 85% priced by 17 September 2026, so the 9 bp rise in the 10-year yield on 18 September 2026 reflects guidance, not the move itself. That distinction matters more than the headline number, and it is the thing I want to unpack here. Markets, as they often do, reacted swiftly. The yen strengthened initially, then gave back some gains as traders digested the details. The 10-year JGB yield ticked up by about 2 basis points, a modest move. But the real action was in the swaps market, where the implied path for the policy rate shifted. Before the meeting, overnight index swaps were pricing in a roughly 40 percent chance of a hike by the end of 2026. After the meeting, that probability rose to around 60 percent. This suggests that market participants interpreted the bank's language as slightly more hawkish than expected. However, I would caution against over-reading a single meeting. The bank has repeatedly stressed that it will be data-dependent, and the next few months of wage and price data will be crucial. For now, I am keeping an open mind. The yen could strengthen further if the BoJ signals a policy shift, or it could weaken if the Fed delays rate cuts. Either way, investors should be prepared for volatility. That is not a prediction; it is a recognition of uncertainty. And in my experience, acknowledging uncertainty is the first step toward managing it. Looking ahead, there are several key events that could shape the BoJ's next move. First, the shunto wage negotiations in spring 2027 will be critical. If wage growth accelerates, the bank may feel more confident about raising rates. Second, the consumption tax hike scheduled for October 2026 could dampen consumer spending, which might make the bank more cautious. Third, global economic conditions, particularly in China and the US, will influence Japan's export sector. Finally, the bank's own communication will be key. Governor Ueda has been careful to avoid surprising markets, but he has also shown a willingness to adjust policy when needed. I would expect the bank to continue with a gradual approach, possibly raising rates once or twice by the end of 2027, but this is highly uncertain. As always, I will be watching the data and the bank's language closely. In conclusion, the BoJ's latest meeting did not bring any policy changes, but it did offer a subtle shift in tone. The bank is slowly moving toward normalization, but it is doing so cautiously. Markets have priced in a higher probability of a rate hike, but they may be getting ahead of themselves. The bank's decisions will depend on a range of factors, including wage growth, inflation, and global conditions. Speaking as an ex-central banker, I've learned to be wary of drawing firm conclusions from short stretches of market action. The yen has strengthened against the dollar in recent weeks, and that move has prompted a familiar debate about whether the long-standing rate differential between Japan and the United States is finally narrowing in a way that matters for investors. I want to separate what has been said by officials from what markets have actually done, because the two are not always aligned. Markets, however, have a habit of running ahead of central banks. The yen's recent appreciation has been driven in part by expectations that the rate differential will narrow, either because the Fed will cut rates or because the BoJ will raise them. But the actual differential remains wide. The 10-year US Treasury yield is still well above the 10-year JGB yield, even after the recent moves. That gap is the compensation for currency risk, and it is why the carry trade persists.

The company also disclosed a gross margin of 48.7 percent, down from 51.2 percent in the same quarter of 2025. Operating income was NT$38.9 billion, and net income was NT$31.4 billion. The filings state that Kestrel's 3-nanometer wafer capacity reached 120,000 wafers per month as of June 30, 2026, up from 95,000 wafers per month at the end of March 2026. The company attributed the increase to the completion of a phase-two expansion at its Fab 18 in Tainan. According to the filing, 5-nanometer capacity remained flat at 150,000 wafers per month. The filing also notes that Kestrel's advanced packaging capacity, specifically its CoWoS line, stood at 35,000 wafers per month at quarter-end, compared to 28,000 wafers per month in the prior quarter. Kestrel stated that it expects CoWoS capacity to reach 45,000 wafers per month by December 31, 2026. No independent verification of these capacity figures was provided in the filing. The filings disclose that Kestrel's average selling price for 3-nanometer wafers increased by 4.2 percent quarter-over-quarter. The filing attributes this increase to a shift in product mix toward higher-priced variants. For 5-nanometer wafers, the average selling price decreased by 1.8 percent. The filing lists two customers that each accounted for more than 10 percent of Kestrel's net revenue in the quarter: Customer A represented 22 percent, and Customer B represented 14 percent. The identities of these customers are redacted in the public version of the filing. Kestrel also reported that its top ten customers accounted for 68 percent of net revenue, up from 65 percent in the prior quarter. Kestrel's filing states that capital expenditure for the quarter was NT$98.7 billion, with 70 percent allocated to advanced nodes and 30 percent to specialty technologies. The company reaffirmed its full-year 2026 capital expenditure guidance of NT$360 billion to NT$380 billion. For the third quarter of 2026, Kestrel provided revenue guidance of NT$148 billion to NT$154 billion, and gross margin guidance of 47.5 percent to 49.5 percent. The filing notes that these projections are forward-looking statements and are subject to risks described in the risk factors section on pages 45 to 52.
